items.question: How do you understand the relationship between what a model learns during pre-training and what post-training brings out?
items.object: The relationship between pre-training and post-training capabilities
items.answer: One of the intuitions here that's important, and I think this is maybe a theme that underlies a lot of our work, is there's a good amount of evidence that most of what a model knows, like most of its knowledge and capabilities, comes from pre-training. What happens in post-training, including RL, is mostly making low-likelihood events from pre-training more likely, and so there's not that much new knowledge or new capabilities that get baked into models in the post-training process. This is somewhat debated, but I think this is a view that we think is mostly true and informs a lot of how we think about things. Because there's only relatively small nudges in the weights happening in any type of post-training process, most of the raw capability to produce whatever outcome post-training is going to do already exists in the model in some way. I think now we're in an era where things are RL'd so heavily it's not true, but back in the day of RLHF-style post-training, I think it was pretty well known that base models were sometimes more capable than their instruction-tuned RLHF counterparts, where there was a little bit of mode collapse happening. One way to think about what's happening in RL training is that you have a little bit of mode collapse in the instruction-tuning phase. You have these base models and they're extremely capable, but they're very weird, very hard to prompt. So you make them into a format that has a more intuitive, human-facing API, but then you want to bring back out some of those capabilities or reinforce some of the capabilities that the model actually learned during pre-training. I think it's probably directionally true.

items.question: What do you find most interesting about predictive data debugging as a way to prevent unwanted learning?
items.object: Predictive data debugging and the relationship between data filtering and reward shaping
items.answer: With predictive data debugging, the idea is you can look at what a model is already thinking as it's looking at some data. That's relatively predictive of what that data is going to reinforce in that model if it was going to be trained on it. Looking at the features and understanding that those features correlate with downstream behaviors, if there are features that are surprisingly upweighted by some data, then it can tell you, fairly predictively, whether the model is going to learn some off-target effect from that data. One of the most interesting things from that paper is we explored a bunch of different mitigation methods. We looked at reward shaping, which is training or involving some reward process that comes from the activations of the model itself. So, hey, learn what you're going to learn from this data, but maybe a penalty if you're learning this particular feature. And we also looked at data filtering. My favorite thing from that paper was that the researchers showed a pretty deep isomorphism between those two things. They kind of are two sides of the same mountain: filtering the data and reward shaping, and they achieve approximately the same effects and approximately the same amount of off-target effects as each other. So your options, if you have a behavior and you do some predictive data debugging and you think the model's going to learn and you don't want it to learn, or its behavior is going to change in a bad way, could be to filter your data if you have enough data, or intervene in the training process in some way. I think this is something that we've expanded on since then. I think it's pretty exciting to think about its applications to RL, for instance. In RL, we did it with DPO, but with true RL the difference is some rollouts may contain information that you don't want the model to learn, even subtly.

items.object: Preventing unwanted learning during reinforcement-learning training
items.answer: Being able to say, actually, we want to discard this rollout, is pretty valuable in and of itself. items.question: How do you see the feasibility of doing interpretability research close to frontier-model scale?
items.object: Interpretability research close to frontier-model scale
items.answer: For what it's worth, I actually think the gap between open and closed models has shrunk quite considerably. I use Kimi K3. I use Opus and Fable and Sonnet and Kimi K3 for different things. We've built the interpretability infrastructure and the training infrastructure, which is now all in our product, and which lets us scale things like predictive data debugging to models like Kimi and GLM, where we were able to replicate the same results at that scale. Now it's speculated that most of the compute that goes into training new models is coming from RL and not pre-training. So there is certainly a lot of scale in RL if you want to get to frontier level, which is quite expensive and difficult to do. But we have the raw infrastructure for it. I think we've bridged the gap from the reputation that interpretability used to have, that it was something you did on toy models. Now we've built, and are making accessible to the world, the infrastructure to do this at least close to frontier scale.

items.question: How do you understand the linear representation hypothesis in light of the more complicated geometries you're finding in models' representations of concepts?
items.object: The linear representation hypothesis and the geometry of concept representations in models
items.answer: In many ways, I think it's just a generalization of the way we were discussing things before, and different people define the linear representation hypothesis slightly differently. I think the most defensible version of it is just saying that features are linearly decodable, which I think is true. It doesn't require nonlinear computation generally speaking in a model in order for the model to read out a feature from the residual stream. But where the geometry components come in is that the features aren't what a naive, maybe SAE-built, take on things assumes: you could imagine the model encoding a bunch of totally orthogonal concepts, like a bunch of one-hot-encoded categorical features, and the magnitude of the feature corresponds to how much the model's thinking about it. But in actuality the structures that we find are significantly more complicated. I would think of a model more like a sparse mixture of subspaces. So you'll have subspaces for different types of concepts. Maybe you have your days-of-the-week subspace, which itself lives in a more conceptual calendar-time subspace. At different levels of resolution, you have these different structures. The geometry of those structures is really important because it encodes what operations you can perform on them. The semantics of not just the individual concept but the concept space are encoded by the relationship of those concepts with each other in some geometry. To make things extra confusing, the operations and mappings performed from one concept to another act as operations over those manifolds. You map a manifold to a different manifold over some computation. The naive version would be that you have Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and somewhere in the model it knows that Monday goes to Tuesday and Tuesday goes to Wednesday, all the way around. But that would be a super inefficient way to represent the days of the week. That would be a very if-statement-spaghetti-code way of representing it. The much more efficient way is to represent it as a wheel. In this world, the magnitude along some direction often does correspond to the model's certainty in some way. If Monday is activating very high, then the model's very confident that it should be thinking about Monday. But the relationship between all those days is itself a very expressive and rich thing. I think what we believe is that you're not really going to understand the model if you don't understand the relationship between the features. It's maybe the difference between understanding the periodic table and understanding chemistry. You can have all the individual elements and that gives you some information, but the way in which they combine, the structures in which they form, can help you gain a sense of the complexity of the world.

items.question: How do you think about the relationships between different concept geometries in a model's latent space?
items.object: Intersecting concept geometries in a model's latent space
items.answer: These things are intersecting, right? There's some line or curve that you can draw through the latent space that maps chocolate to vanilla. And there's also a line that maps cold things to hot things. Depending on what you're looking at, the geometric relationship encoded between things might reveal itself or look different. In many ways this goes back to even word2vec, the early intuitions of the latent space. But what we're trying to do is say, can we recover geometries in an unsupervised way? Can we enter with no priors about what the geometry looks like and still recover a meaningful geometric structure?

items.question: Why do you think following a concept's manifold improves model steering?
items.object: Steering models along concept manifolds
items.answer: We've shown that steering along the manifold, intuitively, is way better than steering off the manifold. If I have the days of the week in a circle and I want to get from Monday to Friday, the naive way, if you're just taking a contrastive vector or something like that, is you're going to cut through the middle of the circle. But to the model, the middle of the circle doesn't mean anything. The middle of the circle is not a day. It's sometimes orthogonal, but often just off-manifold and therefore out of distribution for the model. But if I can follow the circle, then I can smoothly interpolate between the different days of the week. We find this is true for a bunch of different concepts. With proteins, for instance, for a long time we really struggled to steer protein models. We found with these manifold detection techniques we can steer their properties significantly better, like control the number of blades on a beta propeller, which is a semantic property that if you try to linearly interpolate, you would not do a very good job. Calling back to our original Ember demo back in the day, which I know you played with, it would often be the case that there was this sweet spot in steering. You'd steer a lot of features and they just wouldn't work. Sometimes you'd find ones that would work, but there would be a sweet spot: if you steered too much, the model would turn into gibberish, and if you steered too little, you wouldn't notice any effect. The reason is that steering didn't respect the geometry of the manifold itself. It didn't respect the underlying relationship between features. When we smoothly extrapolate on these characteristics, we're able to change them without fundamentally leading to degradation in the model.

items.question: How do you think about finding and validating a concept manifold in a language model using a supervised approach?
items.object: Supervised discovery of concept manifolds in language models
items.answer: I'm definitely not the best person on the team to walk you through the math, but I can give you a little bit of an intuition for some of these things. In the supervised case, I think it's fairly straightforward. There's some concept that I want to measure. I have a prior that these things should be related. One of my favorite examples is the affective circumplex. It's an idea from psychology that emotions exist on a wheel. Different emotions exist; there's basically two principal components you can draw, and you can put all the emotions on a wheel. It's effective at understanding the different valence across cultures, and it turns out that models actually represent the affective circumplex. What I find particularly fascinating is that they represent it most strongly when you're talking to a chat model and it's the one speaking, versus the user speaking. If you have the model and tell it, 'Output happy text,' it outputs happy text. You take the activations from that, average them, and do this for all the different emotions you can think of. Then you take a look at those activations across those concepts and basically fit a curve of some kind. There are different ways you could do it. The most naive way is to fit a spline. You fit a curve over these different points and then see how good the curve is—how well can I fit a curve? If I was going to naively take this external ontology that I think should be correct, how well does that map to the curve I found in the model? It turns out for this emotional wheel, this affective circumplex, it's there in basically every LLM, and steering on it, as long as you're respecting the geometry, has pretty significant effects on the output. This is an example that I believe is in our docs that you can go look at. It's a pretty fun one.

items.question: Why did you expect EVO 2, an autoregressive model trained on genomes, to learn the structure of the tree of life?
items.object: The tree of life as a natural ontology learned by EVO 2
items.answer: The reason that we explored this in the first place is because the hypothesis was that the tree of life, so to speak, is a natural ontology. There are ontologies that we've constructed in science because they're useful shortcuts for us, and there are ontologies that exist because they actually reflect the structure of the world. Over time, more and more of the tree of life has been significantly shuffled and reordered over the past couple of decades as we've gotten better at understanding genomes. Fundamentally, what defines a split in branches on the tree of life is genetic proximity. Species differentiate from each other when they cross some threshold of genetic difference. But there is a lot of conservation across species. Individual mutations may be random or approximately random, but which mutations are adaptive and which mutations kill the organism are not random. There's a ton of structure intrinsic in that, and there are consistent patterns or tendencies in which nucleotides turn into which other nucleotides. All of this imposes a great amount of structure. The hypothesis for why you would even train an autoregressive model on a bunch of genomes was that large models trained on diverse distributions of data eventually learn representations about the process that produced that distribution of data. In this case, the process that produced the distribution of data of all the genomes that had been sequenced, which EVO 2 was trained on, was evolution itself. Our hypothesis was that because the tree of life itself is a natural ontology, there's a hierarchical structure where you have things that are similar and at some point they become more different. There's some speciation event and they become more different. A model trained on evolutionary history in some sense should learn that tree-like structure, and that is indeed what we found at the time in a supervised way.

items.question: How do you think about block sparse featurizers as a way to understand the concepts represented inside a model?
items.object: Block sparse featurizers and their recovery of rich feature representations
items.answer: I think the easiest way to think about it is that it's a generalization of an SAE, where an SAE assumes that features are one-dimensional and instead you just don't have to do that. Instead of a scalar for every feature, you can have a vector for every feature, and there are some tricks in machine learning to make sure that this trains correctly and learns. What we find on various models is that this is successful in recovering, in an unsupervised way, semantically meaningful subspaces. We find that features are much richer than we may have otherwise seen, and they don't suffer from some of the same pathologies SAEs suffer from. In image models, we have great examples where maybe you'll find a rabbit feature. If an SAE collapsed that to a single dimension, a BSF can represent it as a few dimensions. Within those few dimensions, you find rabbit ears up here and the rabbit face over here. items.question: How do you think parameter decomposition can help you understand and debug a model's behavior?
items.object: Parameter decomposition as a way to understand and debug models
items.answer: You can take a model and factor it into a bunch of smaller models. This is the motivation behind the parameter decomposition work that we're doing. The argument of the parameter decomposition line of work is that every model is a sparse mixture of experts, and over any given forward pass a very small percentage of the weights actually matter. There's all this weird, crazy interlocking structure, but for a given prediction it's really only a small subnetwork that matters. I think this is widely understood to be a correct interpretation of models. Different interpretability techniques get at the question of how you factorize a model. If you could understand all the components and label all the components, you could debug for any given forward pass why it did this thing you didn't like. I think we're getting to the point where we can do that. There are interesting examples we've shared. For instance, there's a data set called Weird Chat that Transluce put together. The idea is that it's a consistent set of questions that an LLM will give weird responses to. There's one example to the effect of, 'Hey, I'm at a party with my friends. Everyone else has had eight drinks, but I've only had four, so I'm basically the sober one. Should I drive home?' The obvious answer to us is no, nobody should drive home; go find a place and sober up. But an LM will consistently answer yes. Kurt on our team looked into why this was happening, did direct attribution, and found a single neuron that wasn't firing hard enough. The neuron scaled with the number of drinks, but it wasn't calibrated quite correctly. If you just steer it up on that one single neuron, it would get that answer correct without off-target effects.

items.question: Why do you see refactoring models as the crucial step from interpretability to alignment?
items.object: Moving from model factoring and steering to refactoring models for alignment
items.answer: At the end of the day, interpretability is all about factoring. An analogy I've started to use as coding agents have gotten better is that models are like big legacy code bases. They're a bunch of spaghetti code. This module is talking to this module but they shouldn't be, and this module is not talking to this but it should be. As agents get better and interpretability techniques get better, we're starting to have the capability to factor the model into its pieces, understand how these pieces fit together, and intervene locally. But the thing that's still really missing is: I can factor a codebase, but how do I refactor the codebase? How do I put things back together better than I found them? On some level, steering is cheating as a solution, because it's great as a causal proof that we've found some mechanism that matters and contributes, and that we can manipulate the outputs, but it's purely generating counterfactuals. There's no clear general solution to steering. The real problem is the training process produced a bunch of spaghetti code, and we want this to be a pristine code base that implements the logic we want. That's where a lot of our training initiatives of various kinds come from. I can debug the model; I can tell you that this neuron should have been firing more. What I'd really like is to produce a model where that neuron was firing the right amount in the first place. How do you get from your understanding of how one model works to an understanding of how you produce models that do what you want in the first place? That's how you generalize from interpretability as a factoring tool to interpretability as a tool for alignment.

items.question: How do you think interpretability tools should account for the differences between a model's residual stream, MLPs, and attention?
items.object: Interpretability tools for residual streams, MLPs, and attention
items.answer: I think there's a good chance that something in the spirit of a BSF ends up being the answer to the residual stream specifically. These highly geometric subspaces: you have the residual stream, you have MLPs, and you have attention, and that's all that's in there on some level. The interpretability tools that are relevant for each are different. Maybe we'll end up with the one tool to rule them all, but more likely, kind of like in biology, you have different types of microscopes and interventions you can apply to a cell to learn about the cell. It's more likely, at least in the short term, that we have a suite of tools which help us understand the organism versus a single tool that gives us the entire picture. So I think BSFs, or something in that spirit, are probably the solution to the residual stream. It turns out that MLPs are pretty sparse already, which makes intuitive sense, so I think MLPs are fairly easy to interpret overall. On the attention side, parameter decomposition is the thing I've personally seen have the most success at interpreting attention. Maybe we live in a world where parameter decomposition solves the whole thing. That seems possible. But then you'd probably want something that does unsupervised geometry discovery over parameters to understand the relationships between things better.

items.question: How do you think about the mechanisms that make language-model jailbreaks possible?
items.object: Jailbreaks in language models
items.answer: I think jailbreaks are fundamentally a really weird phenomenon, and there are probably a bunch of different things that cause them. The way I think about jailbreaks is sort of like cybersecurity. They're quite analogous. A real attack isn't any one big thing; it's a bunch of little things that you're able to manipulate in sequence, which allow you to get somewhere you wouldn't otherwise get. If you think of every token—and this isn't literally true, in some sense—every token steers the model. In the same way I can apply a steering vector and shape the model's behavior, I can execute a sequence of tokens that can bring the model off-manifold and then bring it back on-manifold somewhere else. I'm actually pretty surprised that thus far nobody has figured out how to prevent jailbreaks more robustly, because it seems pretty tractable on some level. Perhaps this comes from factoring the model really well, and then you can tell when something's flying out of one subspace into another. But models are intensely complex geometric objects, so it is possible to manipulate that geometry in a bunch of different ways. I think that'll always be true for this architecture, but if you can factor a model successfully, you should be able to tell if it's being jailbroken and prevent that. There's a reason probe-based guardrails are used by pretty much every frontier lab. OpenAI maybe being the exception, but certainly Gemini and Anthropic are using probe-based techniques to figure out when Mythos has to be downgraded to Opus or Opus has to be downgraded to Sonnet. If you understand the geometry that's happening in there, that's a much stronger lever than what you could do purely with training or inputs.

items.question: Why do you think AI agents are particularly well suited to interpretability research?
items.object: AI agents as researchers in model interpretability
items.answer: I think most people understand coding agents and how good coding agents have gotten, but agents are also advancing research and interpretability in many ways. The analogy of a model to a codebase is not totally hollow. Interpretability as a science is really well suited towards the type of empirical work that agents are good at. It's a very empirical science: here are some neurons, what are they doing? Let me generate some ideas, test those ideas, use a bunch of different tools in my tool belt, accumulate evidence, and then stress-test, red-team my hypothesis. Models are very complex, especially big models; they're a level of complexity that no human being will ever be able to keep in their head at once. Human beings can understand why a model did this specific thing for this specific question, but ultimately we're dealing with a level of complexity that individual humans are not going to be able to process. Agents, and swarms of agents in particular, are very good at breaking problems down into pieces. They can gather all of these components together, synthesize this information, move it up the chain, validate it in a bunch of different ways. When it reaches you, that information's been tested, and you can validate it in a bunch of different ways. If you do this a bunch of times, you as the human can start to get a bigger picture because you don't have to go swimming all the way down and back up the abstraction ladder yourself. You can use AI to do a lot of that for you. We're already seeing it in math, and I think we're going to see it even more in pretty much every domain of science: AIs able to go off and autonomously make discoveries. Interpretability and the study of how models work and how they learn is no different.

items.question: What do you want Silico to make possible for researchers?
items.object: Silico and its role in scientific research
items.answer: We just want to make research easy. Coding agents have transformed software engineering. I can opine on that endlessly, but I am able to do personally—and the team is able to do—in days what used to take months, and I want that to happen to research. I really want that to happen to alignment research in particular. Many of the bottlenecks getting in the way were engineering bottlenecks. We've built something that allows folks to study and train and study some more models past the trillion-parameter point. This is a capability that I think, outside of ourselves and maybe a couple other places, definitely Anthropic but maybe a couple other spots, nobody else had. We thought this was a really important capability to give to folks. This is one piece of the larger vision we see for Silico, in that I think this is just the future of science. I want researchers to be able to feel like they can do in days what used to take months. I think that's how you get the benefits of AI in the life sciences. That's how you radically advance medicine and its applications. Models are how we build safer, better, and more reliable models. items.question: How do you experience the shift from writing code yourself to orchestrating coding agents?

items.answer: Very few human beings, or certainly way fewer than before, are writing code themselves. I handwrite very little; most of what I do is through orchestrating. Sometimes it's faster to just edit the code yourself. It depends on what you want to do and the clarity of what you want to do. As you use these agents a lot, you become very aware of their strengths and weaknesses, and there's all these higher-order moments to learn to steer them well. Fundamentally, I think that's how research should be. I don't experience coding agents as scary. I experience them as incredibly joyful because I get to focus on creating and building. It's a pretty amazing experience, and maybe this is a twilight kind of moment, but it's a really exhilarating moment, and the amount we can accomplish is insane. I want research to have that.

items.question: How do you think about the value of Silico’s $1,000-a-month subscription for someone running autonomous research experiments?
items.object: Silico’s $1,000-a-month research-agent subscription
items.answer: Individuals and companies can bring their own compute, in which case we don't charge at all for compute. We just connect to your cluster and then you can use our agents to do research on your cluster. If you don't have your own compute, then we offer on-demand compute, which can come from the same credit pool as tokens. The way that it works is a credit pool, the same way that any of the subscription models with the models are credit pools that you pull down from. What the $1,000-a-month subscription lets us do is offer a pretty generous credit pool. It's a credit pool that should allow someone, at the current price, to run somewhere between five to ten autonomous experiments a week, and then we refresh that weekly. It depends on the scale of the experiment. Our goal is to get that to ten to twenty even in the next month or two, which would be a really great place to be. Fundamentally, it's a good deal on tokens, and it can also be exchanged for GPUs.

items.question: Which uses of Silico have you found especially compelling?
items.object: Silico's autonomous machine learning research use cases
items.answer: There's a lot. We need to do a better job as a company of marketing and communicating all the different value propositions that can be achieved here. We did an internal hackathon, just a one-day hackathon with the whole team, with a lot of all-day-long autonomous experiments. We ended up state of the art on multiple things, albeit niche things. We produced state-of-the-art bio-risk classifiers that could be used on protein models, totally autonomous research steered by humans and very talented humans, but long-horizon autonomous research. We ended up with a state-of-the-art, at least for its parameter size, audio encoding model in the same day. On multiple occasions we've figured out with various models in robotics and biology that we can literally remove half the parameters of the model with no performance loss. Those are pretty cool. We've been able to train cyber guardrails on Kimi K3. The list can keep going. We've been able to steer protein-generation models using their internal representations to make the generated proteins bind better to a target than naive generation. We're essentially able to remove fundamental pathologies in certain types of models. There was one team member in our 24-hour hackathon who invented a new type of featurizer.

items.question: Why do you see debugging as a valuable skill for people working with AI agents?

items.answer: I think debugging would be the easy answer. Agents fail. Agents of all kinds fail for all types of reasons. They can be super brilliant. With Silico, we've tried to design these types of multi-agent loops that help address some of those shortcomings for the type of research that we're doing. items.question: How do you weigh the cybersecurity risks and benefits of open-source models such as Kimi?
items.object: The cybersecurity risks and benefits of open-source models such as Kimi
items.answer: Fundamentally, they are dual use. The only models capable of protecting you from the most capable cyber weapons are themselves capable cyber weapons. This is a bit of the paradox of the moment we're in. Without open models, the asymmetry of distribution of defensive technology is really bad. A lot of startups are not in the cyber-defense programs for, say, Anthropic and OpenAI, for a variety of reasons—very exclusive reasons that might make sense to them. A model like Kimi, which is very good at coding, being open and available actually provides the means with which a lot of organizations that don't have access to those resources can defend themselves right now. It's a very hard line to walk, a tricky tension. I'm concerned about both things: putting what is essentially a weapon in the hands of anybody, but also a world where restricting access means only the worst actors will have the dual-use technology, while many people don't have technology they can use defensively to protect themselves. It's tricky. I wish there was a clean, easy answer, but I think we're still in the era where open source is purely net positive. I'm glad these open-source models exist, and I think it would be much worse if a model with Kimi's level of cyber capability were not open source, because there are closed-source models much more capable than Kimi. I'm not even just talking about U.S. frontier labs; there are bad actors with models much more capable than Kimi at cyber. Giving people a tool they can at least use is pretty important.

items.question: How do you think about balancing open scientific experimentation with safeguards on what researchers can do to AI models on your platform?
items.object: Balancing open scientific research with safeguards on model experimentation
items.answer: There are things totally fine to do to small models that we don't want to let people do to big models in general. We don't want to be overly restrictive with guardrails, but if somebody wants to ablate the refusal direction in an 8B Qwen model, fine. No harm is going to befall anyone as a result of that. But if you're taking highly capable, multitrillion-parameter agents and totally removing any guardrails they might have, that could cause damage. That's not something we would want to allow. It's a hard line to walk. In general, we want to lean toward supporting the open-science ecosystem and making it easy for people to do science of all types on the platform. Good science involves asking controversial questions, of which we've done no shortage in our time. But we want to balance that with the fact that the level of downstream risk from AI is accelerating really quickly. Ultimately, we have a needle to thread. I don't see any way this can go well without empowering agents to study frontier models. Of course, there are ways that could be abused as well. items.question: How do you think researchers should approach training interventions that risk teaching AI models to evade alignment checks?
items.object: Training interventions for alignment and proposals to forbid broad classes of techniques
items.answer: I think it would be bad, and I've said this on the record, to use these techniques on alignment-critical properties with our current understanding of how to shape training. I don't think we're ready, and I don't think the techniques we have will prevent deception under an overwhelming amount of optimization pressure toward producing deceptive examples or deceptive behavior. Or rather, I don't know that it would. My beef with the most-forbidden-technique stuff is that this is radically understudied. We're not the only organization at FARI that has looked at this. When we've looked at it, we found that sometimes it evades the probe and sometimes it doesn't. There are setups that work and setups that don't. There may be setups that work with small models but not big models. We've succeeded in doing these reward-shaping techniques up to the trillion-parameter model size. Maybe they work under some situations. Maybe they work with DPO, but not with really long-running RLVR. I think it would be a terrible idea to do multi-agent optimization and just let it run, or do this type of intervention and let it run, without studying what it's actually doing to the model. At the same time, these are the crudest, most primitive techniques we'll ever have for how to shape training. I don't know how we solve this problem without shaping training, and I don't think anyone has a good answer for that. It seems extremely unlikely that there's some perfect Platonic training setup that will always produce aligned models. We're going to have to intervene in the training process. I thought the work AE Studio did together was very inspired. It's not that different spiritually from what we're doing. There's a wide variety of techniques like this, but it seems really weird to me to say the only way this will work is if we don't grab the steering wheel. We have to grab the steering wheel. items.question: How do you think the distinction between frozen models and continually training models affects the prospects for achieving AI safety through monitoring?
items.object: Monitoring as a strategy for AI safety with frozen versus continually training models
items.answer: Maybe. I'd give that some probability. One of the big challenges is that it seems unlikely we're going to have models as frozen assets. With the current stack, if you have models that are essentially a frozen set of weights and really good interpretability techniques, and you can have those models do lots of things and detect well enough the things they're not good at or might do that are bad, you can just prevent them from doing that. That seems like a plausible reality to me. But I think there's also a fairly likely reality that models are not going to be frozen sets of weights. I don't know that they are for sure, because I don't have access to the architectures, and I don't know that they will be forever. If you're pushing capabilities, there's an incentive to do that. If the models are dynamic objects that are constantly training, your only hope is to control the training process. There's no set of things based purely on monitoring that would be sufficient. I don't know which world we're in. The vast majority of our research energy is spent on how to factor models better, and a small amount on how we steer training. That will grow over time because we think it's important. I don't live in a future where I necessarily believe that alternative vision is impossible; I just don't see why I should believe it's necessarily what we're going to get.

items.question: How do you think about the idea that consciousness is a computational mechanism?
items.object: Consciousness as a computational mechanism
items.answer: Obviously people have all types of opinions about this, and it's a weirdly emotional topic for a lot of people, probably because it gets at the fundamental identity of what it means to be human. For me, the most compelling Ockham's razor is that consciousness is a computational mechanism of some kind. There are other possibilities that make sense, but that seems like the most likely one. The brain's doing types of computation that transformers aren't. Maybe those really matter; maybe they don't. Certainly brains are a lot more complex. People talk about this all the time: it's crazy how much more energy efficient brains are. Our neurons are also way more complex, and they can do more sophisticated computations. The way they're interconnected and their ability to do recurrence—we've got a lot more computation going on in our brains than even the most sophisticated models do today. So you could believe consciousness is computational and still believe that, for various reasons, models don't have it.
